records.claim: The register tracking table updates are triggered at instruction decode, execution completion, and instruction step decay.
records.quote: At decode, an instruction that writes a register stores its ROB index as a tag in the corresponding entry and clears the valid bit. When the instruction completes, we overwrite the payload with the digest of the produced value and set the valid bit.
records.why: This establishes that the tracking table update logic is triggered at the instruction decode and execution completion stages.

records.claim: The register tracking table update logic is triggered on pipeline flushes to recover in-flight entries.
records.quote: Integrating the path for sending register digests from the execution unit to the predictor and recovering the Tomasulo-like table may present some challenges; we plan to address these in future work.
records.why: The paper explicitly states that recovering the Tomasulo-like table across flushes is an open challenge left for future work rather than an implemented pipeline flush trigger.
records.open_question: Should pipeline flush trigger recovery of the register tracking table, or is recovery omitted as described in the paper's future work?

records.claim: The decay counter decrements for all valid entries on each decoded instruction and clears the valid bit when the counter reaches zero.
records.quote: Consequently, RUNLTS invalidates each digest after 256 subsequent instructions have been decoded, ensuring that only up-to-date information influences future predictions.
records.why: This settles that digests have a lifetime of 256 decoded instructions, decremented on each decode and invalidated when the count expires.

records.claim: At decode, an instruction writing a destination register clears the valid bit, records its 14-bit ROB index in the payload, and initializes the decay counter to 255.
records.quote: At decode, an instruction that writes a register stores its ROB index as a tag in the corresponding entry and clears the valid bit.
records.why: This confirms that at decode, destination register entries are invalidated and tagged with the producing instruction's ROB index.

records.claim: The field inst.rob_idx read by register_tracking_update is context metadata supplied by the host pipeline at decode and completion rather than written by a predictor algorithm.
records.quote: At decode, an instruction that writes a register stores its ROB index as a tag in the corresponding entry and clears the valid bit.
records.why: The paper identifies the tag as the instruction's ROB index, which is standard pipeline context allocated by the host processor.

records.claim: The event handlers on decode and on execution_complete represent host pipeline interface hooks rather than undefined helper functions.
records.quote: At decode, an instruction that writes a register stores its ROB index as a tag in the corresponding entry and clears the valid bit. When the instruction completes, we overwrite the payload with the digest of the produced value and set the valid bit.
records.why: This demonstrates that decode and execution completion are pipeline stage events provided by the host execution environment.

records.claim: When an instruction completes execution matching the in-flight tag, the payload is updated with the generated digest, marked valid, and given a full decay lifetime.
records.quote: When the instruction completes, we overwrite the payload with the digest of the produced value and set the valid bit.
records.why: This settles that instruction completion overwrites the payload with the produced digest and marks the entry valid.

records.claim: On a pipeline flush, in-flight entries whose tags match squashed instructions are identified by a squashed() helper and have their payload cleared.
records.quote: Integrating the path for sending register digests from the execution unit to the predictor and recovering the Tomasulo-like table may present some challenges; we plan to address these in future work.

records.claim: fp64_digest_generation_extraction tests that FP64 extracts bits [63:55] placed at digest bits [11:3] with bits [2:0] zeroed.

records.claim: digest_decay_invalidation tests that a valid register digest transitions from valid=1 to valid=0 after exactly 256 decoded instructions.
records.quote: Consequently, RUNLTS invalidates each digest after 256 subsequent instructions have been decoded, ensuring that only up-to-date information influences future predictions.
records.why: Section 4.2 states that RUNLTS invalidates each digest after 256 subsequent instructions have been decoded.

records.claim: bank_usefulness_scaling_zero_suppression tests that non-positive usefulness selects x0 scaling, suppressing bank contribution to 0.
records.quote: That Sigma feeds a multiplier stage labelled "x0 or x2.5".
records.why: Figure 5(c) specifies the per-bank multiplier stage selecting x0 or x2.5, suppressing non-positive usefulness to 0.

records.claim: single_write_port_random_selection tests that training randomly selects exactly one available register per bank, requiring only a single write port per table.
records.quote: If several registers were available within the same bank, it randomly selects one of them for the update. Owing to this training method, each table in the register component also needs just a single write port.
records.why: Section 4.2 explicitly requires random selection of one available register per bank during training to enable single-port memory implementation.

records.claim: The sR component extends TAGE-SC-L's statistical corrector to exploit register value correlations using 12-bit digests and 8 banks.
records.quote: We propose a novel prediction method that exploits correlations between register values and branch directions (Section 4.2). Our method generates a short digest characterizing each register value and improves prediction accuracy by capturing correlations between these digests and branch directions. We implemented this method by integrating it into the statistical corrector (SC) of the existing TAGE-SC-L predictor.
records.why: Section 1 introduces sR as a novel SC component capturing correlations between register values and branch directions via short digests.

records.claim: Register values available after pipeline flushes allow sR to correct subsequent mispredictions starting with the second one.
records.quote: By leveraging these extra values after the flush, our scheme can correct subsequent mispredictions starting with the second one.
records.why: Section 4.2 describes how values available after a branch flush allow correcting subsequent mispredictions.

records.claim: The spec source citation identifies the CBP 2025 paper 'RUNLTS: Register-value-aware Predictor Utilizing Nested Large Tables'.
records.quote: RUNLTS: Register-value-aware Predictor Utilizing Nested Large Tables
records.why: The paper title verbatim matches the cited source publication.

records.claim: Host interface requires decode-stage register rename/allocation events and backend completion broadcasts to update the Tomasulo-like tracking table.
records.quote: At decode, an instruction that writes a register stores its ROB index as a tag in the corresponding entry and clears the valid bit. When the instruction completes, we overwrite the payload with the digest of the produced value and set the valid bit.
records.why: Section 4.2 details the tracking table interface events at decode and completion.

records.claim: The fallback strategies described for host interfaces (such as updating only at architectural commit or decrementing on branch arrivals) are not part of the paper's design.
records.open_question: The proposed fallback interfaces for systems lacking early execution broadcast or decode-time tracking are implementation accommodations not described in the paper.

records.claim: sR total storage is 53,863 bits (43,008 bits WT, 9,360 bits UT, and 1,495 bits register tracking table).

records.claim: Single-port RAMs suffice for WT and UT tables due to the single-register random selection during training.

records.claim: The default weight width for sR prediction weight tables (WT) and usefulness tables (UT) is 6 bits.

records.claim: The parameter tuning range [5, 8] for weight_bits is not specified in the paper.

records.claim: The parameter algorithms_1_pseudocode_variant captures ambiguous behavior for clearing invalid tags or tracking entries upon pipeline squash.
records.quote: Integrating the path for sending register digests from the execution unit to the predictor and recovering the Tomasulo-like table may present some challenges; we plan to address these in future work.
records.why: Section 5 explicitly leaves recovering the Tomasulo-like table to future work, leaving squash tag clearing undefined.
records.open_question: The paper does not detail how the register tracking table clears invalid tags or handles squash recovery, leaving table recovery to future work.

records.claim: The parameter algorithms_3_pseudocode_variant specifies semantic choices for updating the usefulness tables (UT) during training.
records.quote: During training, we update the correlations only for logical registers that were available at prediction time. If several registers were available within the same bank, it randomly selects one of them for the update.
records.why: Section 4.2 specifies updating correlations for available registers, but does not provide the exact mathematical rule for updating usefulness counters.
records.open_question: The paper states that correlations are updated for available registers but does not define the exact mathematical update rule for usefulness tables.
